items.q: What is a Bitcoin transaction, in the chapter's definition?
options: A message from Alice to Bob that carries the bitcoins
The data Alice uses to convince full nodes to update their database of coin ownership
A record of Alice's balance signed by her wallet
rationales: Bitcoins are not sent to Bob; full nodes are convinced to change their records, and Bob's software reads the shared record.
A transaction names outputs and new conditions, never a balance.

items.q: Alice's transaction is 388 hexadecimal characters. How many bytes is that, and how many weight units?
options: 388 bytes and 1,552 weight
194 bytes and 569 weight
194 bytes and 776 weight
rationales: Two hexadecimal characters make one byte, so 388 characters are 194 bytes.
Weight counts the 125 legacy bytes four times and the 69 segwit bytes once: 500 plus 69 is 569.

items.q: The byte after the version of a transaction is 0x00. What does a modern parser conclude?
options: The transaction has no inputs and is invalid
The transaction is in the extended format: a marker, then a flag, then the real input count
The version field is five bytes long
rationales: A legacy parser would read zero inputs, which no transaction can have; that impossibility is what makes the byte a signal.
The version is always exactly four bytes.

items.q: An input's sequence is 30 in a version 2 transaction, and the output it spends was confirmed at height 774,958. What is the earliest block that can confirm the spend?
rationales: A sequence below 2 to the 31 in a version 2 transaction is a relative timelock, not an ordinary input.
The lock is 30 blocks: 774,958 plus 30 is 774,988, with 29 blocks strictly between.

items.q: Which sequence value does NOT signal BIP125 replaceability?
options: 0xfffffffd
0xfffffffe
rationales: 0xfffffffd is the highest value that signals: at least two below the maximum.
Zero is far below the threshold and signals.

items.q: A third party replaces OP_2 with OP_PUSH1 0x02 in the input script of Alice's legacy transaction. What changes?
options: Nothing: both encodings put the same number on the stack
The transaction identifier, so a transaction Bob built on the original output can become invalid
The signature becomes invalid and the transaction is rejected
rationales: The script result is the same, but the txid is a hash of the bytes, and the bytes differ.
A legacy signature cannot cover the input script that contains it, so it stays valid.

items.q: Why could segregated witness be deployed as a soft fork?
options: Because old nodes see a segwit output as anyone-can-spend and accept an empty input script, while new nodes require a valid witness
Because every node upgraded on the same day
Because the witness structure is included in the legacy serialization
rationales: New rules only reject more than old rules did, which is the definition of a soft fork.
The witness is excluded from the legacy serialization and from the txid.

items.q: The chapter says Alice's transaction is in block 774,958. What did two explorers report?
options: The same block, 774,958
Block 775,072; 774,958 is the block of the transaction her input spends
Block 774,957, the lock time of the previous transaction
rationales: mempool.space and blockstream.info both place 46620030... in block 775,072.
774,957 is the lock time of the previous transaction, not a block it is in.
